company.sector: Renewable power (wind, solar, hydro, battery storage; Sri Lanka, Uganda, Pakistan)

summary.headline: Sri Lanka's biggest private wind producer, building fast on borrowed money, at 1.9x book for a 6–8% return
summary.text: WindForce PLC (WIND.N0000) owns 253 MW of wind, solar and hydro plants (152 MW its own share) and is more than doubling that with 130 MW of battery storage, a 100 MW solar park and a 10 MW wind farm, about Rs 71bn of projects. It passes three of the four business tests (debt, steady profit, cash) but fails the most important one: return on equity has been only 6–8% a year for five years, well below the 16.3% a shareholder should demand. Owners' profit for the half to September 2026 rose 7% to Rs 1.61bn (EPS Rs 1.19), but net debt jumped from Rs 6.6bn to Rs 24.9bn in six months to pay for projects that earn nothing yet, and no dividend has been paid since 2024/25. Most of the older wind farms were built in 2010–2014 on 20-year contracts that the company says generally can't be extended for wind. At Rs 38.00 the share is 1.9x NAV of Rs 19.92 and 31x the last 12 months' EPS. Five methods put fair value at about Rs 6.50. I'd buy at up to Rs 5.54 and treat Rs 4.88 or less as a strong buy. Watch list (category 2).

quality.reason: Moderate debt, five years of profits and good cash generation, but returns on equity of only 6–8%.

tests.label: Return on equity of 15% or more
tests.note: About 6.8%, 6.8%, 7.7% and 6.3% for 2022/23–2025/26 (owners' profit ÷ average owners' equity, worked out); about 6.3% for the last 12 months. Well below 15% and below the 16.3% cost of equity.

tests.label: Net debt no more than equity
tests.note: Net debt Rs 24.89bn at 30 September 2026 against owners' equity Rs 27.0bn (0.26x in March; 0.76x total equity including minorities). Close to the limit, and about 5x 2025/26 EBITDA while the new plants are being built (the company's own figure was 1.39x in March).

tests.label: Steady profit: no loss in five years, no one-offs
tests.note: No loss in five years. 2024/25 was lifted by Rs 1.19bn of one-offs (tariff arrears and a gain on selling rooftop solar); on the company's normalised basis group profit rose to Rs 2.14bn in 2025/26 from Rs 1.32bn.

tests.label: Profit turns into cash and dividends
tests.value: Cash before working capital Rs 4.93bn vs profit Rs 2.15bn (2025/26)
tests.note: Depreciation-heavy plants turn profit into cash: cash generated from operations Rs 5.12bn (2024/25) and Rs 3.08bn (2025/26, after Rs 1.85bn tied up in receivables). Rs 1.00 dividend for 2024/25, but none for 2025/26 or so far in 2026/27 while cash goes into projects.

highlights.title: Six months to 30 September 2026 (unaudited)

highlights.title: Borrowing for the next stage
highlights.text: Net debt rose from Rs 6.63bn to Rs 24.89bn in six months: Rs 12.7bn of plant and a Rs 9.2bn rise in project advances, mainly the 13-site, 130 MW / 520 MWh battery storage programme (Rs 22.5bn, 51% owned with Vidullanka). The first 10 MW battery site and the 5 MW Diya Janani floating solar plant were commissioned in September 2026; the other 12 battery sites are due by December 2026.

Low for five years and well below the 16.3% cost of equity, so on today's returns the business is worth less than book.
A justified forward P/E of about 4–6x at a 16.3% cost of equity and 6–10% ROE.

Cash before interest after upkeep from today's plants. With the projects at cost and net debt of Rs 24.9bn taken off, about Rs 9.9 a share.

models.name: Whole-company DCF (WACC, less net debt) + projects and joint ventures
models.comment: Existing consolidated plants valued as a whole company: cash before interest after maintenance capex Rs 1.6 / 2.35 / 2.7bn (cash from operations before working capital of about Rs 4.6 / 4.9 / 5.1bn, less tax of Rs 0.6 / 0.5 / 0.45bn, less maintenance Rs 2.4 / 2.0 / 1.88bn), after-tax operating profit Rs 2.10 / 2.48 / 2.71bn (operating profit excluding joint ventures and goodwill impairment of about Rs 2.8 / 3.1 / 3.3bn, taxed at 25 / 20 / 18%), growing 0% / 3% / 6% for five years then 1% / 3% / 4%, less the reinvestment that growth needs at an 8% / 10% / 12% return on capital, discounted at WACC 14.5% / 13.5% / 12.5% (scripts/reinvestment.py). Firm value Rs 10.5 / 15.8 / 22.0bn; value after year 5 is 48% / 62% / 74%. Less net debt Rs 24.89bn at 30 September 2026, which already includes the borrowing for projects still being built, so those are added back at cost: Rs 21.9bn (half-year capex Rs 12.7bn plus the Rs 9.2bn rise in project advances, mainly the 130 MW battery storage programme and the 10 MW Safe Power wind farm) at 85% / 100% / 120% of cost, and joint ventures (Rs 6.57bn book, including the 100 MW Rividhanavi solar park) at 85% / 100% / 125% of book. Less minorities at book (Rs 5.94bn). Equity Rs 3.9 / 13.4 / 25.6bn, or Rs 2.86 / 9.88 / 18.91 a share. The calculator's own start cash (Rs −0.8 / 0.4 / 0.5bn from 2025/26 operating cash) isn't used because Rs 1.85bn was tied up in late CEB payments and project advances that year. The perpetuity assumes the older wind farms are repowered when their contracts end (2030–2034 if the 20-year terms run from commissioning); the bear's 0% growth allows for that cost.

models.name: P/E method
models.comment: EPS for the year to March 2027 of Rs 1.20 / 1.35 / 1.55 times 4.24 / 4.51 / 5.53, the forward P/E justified at the cost of equity (17.8 / 16.3 / 14.8%) when growth is paid for (payout = 1 − growth ÷ ROE; ROE 6 / 7.5 / 10%, growth 2 / 3 / 4%). Base EPS is 46% below the Rs 2.52 'latest quarter × 4' run-rate because the September quarter is the windy peak (south-west monsoon): in 2025/26 the first half earned Rs 1.11 and the second half only Rs 0.03. It is 11% above the Rs 1.22 earned in the last 12 months. The base allows Rs 0.16 for the second half, including the first battery sites (from October 2026) against higher finance costs.

models.name: Justified P/B
models.comment: (ROE − growth) ÷ (cost of equity − growth) × NAV Rs 19.92: ROE 6 / 7.5 / 10%, growth 2 / 3 / 4%, cost of equity 17.8 / 16.3 / 14.8%. ROE has been 6–8% for five years, well below the cost of equity, so the business is worth less than its book value until new projects lift returns. Rs 38.00 would need a lasting ROE of about 28%.

models.name: Residual income
models.comment: Book value Rs 19.92 (September 2026). ROE moves from 6.3% (last 12 months) to 6 / 7.5 / 10% over ten years, with 35% paid out, at a cost of equity of 17.8 / 16.3 / 14.8%; after that the (negative) excess return grows at 2 / 3 / 4%. Every year subtracts value because ROE stays below the cost of equity; the lowest method after dividends. (On 17 November this was worked by hand with no excess return after year 10, giving Rs 10.84.)

models.name: Dividends (two-stage)
models.comment: No dividend for 2025/26 or so far in 2026/27 (Rs 1.00 for 2024/25). Assumes Rs 0.25 / 0.50 / 1.00 a year from next year, growing 2 / 4 / 6% for five years (below the 6.3% supported by ROE with all profit kept) then 2 / 3 / 4%, at the cost of equity. The dividend is at risk while cash and new debt go into projects.

modelsNote: A contracted power producer suits a whole-company DCF; projects still being built are added at cost (their debt is already in net debt) and joint ventures at book. P/E, justified P/B, residual income and dividends use the cost of equity and come from scripts/valuation.py. Growth check: assumed 0% / 3% / 6% against 6.8% supported (reinvestment rate 83.9% × return on capital 8.2%, FY2026); all within it. The bigger growth from the Rs 71bn pipeline is valued through the projects at cost, not by raising the growth rate.

scenarios.common: Net debt Rs 24.89bn, NAV Rs 19.92 and minorities Rs 5.94bn at 30 September 2026. 1,355.4 million shares. Price Rs 38.00 (18 Nov 2026). Older wind plants (2010–2014) are on 20-year contracts; the bear assumes no growth from today's plants.

sensitivity.title: Justified price to book, Rs per share
sensitivity.note: Growth 3%, NAV Rs 19.92. Rs 38.00 would need a lasting ROE of about 28% at a 16.3% cost of equity.

buyPlan.note: About Rs 2,620 in total, against Rs 19,000 at Rs 38.00.
buyPlan.realism: Rs 5.54 needs a fall of about 85%. The share traded at Rs 38.50–41.90 in the September quarter and Rs 22.90–56.10 in the year to March 2026, so it isn't likely. Even the lowest price of the past 18 months is about four times the buy price.

higher: Battery storage sites earning well above the cost of capital once all 13 are running (from December 2026).
Rividhanavi and Safe Power finished on time and budget, lifting group ROE towards 12% or more.
Older wind farms (2010–2014, on 20-year contracts) repowered or re-contracted on good terms.
The CEB/NSO paying on time and paying curtailment compensation.
lower: ROE staying at 6–8% after the new plants start.
Debt rising further, or finance costs outgrowing new revenue.
Wind contracts expiring without renewal, or tariff cuts.
More curtailment, or poor wind and rain.
Cost overruns on Rividhanavi (a US$133mn project held 50%).

notes.disclaimer: These are estimates from the Annual Report 2025/26 and the interim report to 30 September 2026, at the CSE close of 18 November 2026. Beta inputs are provisional web-search figures. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.

fullText:
WINDFORCE PLC (WIND.N0000): long-term valuation, 2026-11-18 (full redo)

SUMMARY
WindForce is Sri Lanka's largest private wind power producer, with 253 MW of wind, solar and hydro plants (152 MW its own share) in Sri Lanka, Uganda and Pakistan. It is building fast: 130 MW of grid battery storage, a 100 MW solar park and a 10 MW wind farm, about Rs 71bn of projects. It passes three of the four business tests (debt, steady profit, cash), so it counts as "good", but it fails the most important one: return on equity has been only 6–8% a year for five years, against a 16.3% cost of equity. At Rs 38.00 (CSE close, 18 November 2026) the share is 1.9x NAV of Rs 19.92 and 31x the last 12 months' EPS of Rs 1.22. On five methods fair value is about Rs 6.50 (Rs 6.51). I'd buy at up to Rs 5.54 and treat Rs 4.88 or less as a strong buy. The price assumes the new projects will earn far more than WindForce's plants have so far. Watch list (category 2).

THE BUSINESS
- Wind (84 MW in Sri Lanka, about half the country's private wind capacity): revenue Rs 3.18bn in 2025/26. Seven farms: Seguwantivu and Vidatamunai (2010), Daily Life, Powergen and Nirmalapura (49%, 2012), Joule and Beta (66.4%, 2014), and Hiruras (15 MW, 2023). The report names the "impending expiry of power purchase agreements for select assets" as a weakness, says extending wind contracts is generally not feasible, and plans to repower older farms. Contracts are 20-year; if they run from commissioning, the 2010 farms end around 2030, the 2012 farms around 2032 and the 2014 farms around 2034 (the report doesn't give the dates).
- Solar (13 plants, including the 10 MW Sooryashakthi plant added in 2025/26 and the 5 MW Diya Janani floating plant in September 2026): revenue Rs 2.02bn, the most profitable segment.
- Hydro: revenue Rs 0.39bn. All expiring hydro contracts were renewed for 20 years in 2024/25.
- Overseas: Tororo solar in Uganda (subsidiary) Rs 1.05bn revenue; joint ventures Gharo Solar in Pakistan (30%) and Ziba in Uganda (25.5%).
- New: 13 battery storage (BESS) sites, 130 MW / 520 MWh, under 15-year build-own-operate contracts with the National System Operator, Rs 22.5bn, mostly through Storex (51% WindForce, 49% Vidullanka). Rividhanavi, a 100 MW solar park (50/50 joint venture, about US$133mn). Safe Power, a 10 MW wind farm (51%, Rs 4.2bn). Lowest bidder for the 50 MW Mullikulam wind project.
- Small lines: engineering (EPC) and electric two-wheelers.
- Buyers: the CEB and its National System Operator. Payments were late in 2025/26, and the grid curtailed output at weekends (Rs 194mn of revenue lost in the half to September 2026; compensation approved in principle but not yet paid).

LATEST RESULTS
Six months to 30 September 2026 (unaudited): revenue Rs 5.61bn (+20%), gross profit Rs 3.21bn (+12%), operating profit Rs 2.43bn (+13%), finance costs Rs 634mn (+43%), joint ventures Rs 348mn (+25%), owners' profit Rs 1.61bn (+7%), EPS Rs 1.19 (Rs 1.11). September quarter: revenue Rs 2.99bn (+17%), owners' profit Rs 848mn (+11%), EPS Rs 0.63.
The balance sheet changed a lot. Plant rose from Rs 24.8bn to Rs 36.4bn and project advances from Rs 1.7bn to Rs 10.9bn, paid for by Rs 19.0bn of new loans and Rs 2.23bn from Storex's partner. Net debt went from Rs 6.63bn to Rs 24.89bn. Cash from operations was −Rs 6.99bn because the project advances pass through receivables.
Results are seasonal: the south-west monsoon makes April–September the windy half. In 2025/26 the first half earned EPS Rs 1.11 and the second half only Rs 0.03.

2025/26 (audited): revenue Rs 8.04bn (+16%), operating profit Rs 2.75bn, owners' profit Rs 1.54bn (−14%), EPS Rs 1.14. 2024/25 had Rs 1.19bn of one-offs (Rs 708mn tariff arrears and Rs 486mn gain on selling rooftop solar); on the company's normalised basis, group profit rose 62% to Rs 2.14bn. No dividend (Rs 1.00 a year earlier). Effective tax 12.3%, helped by capital allowances.

BUSINESS TESTS (3 of 4: good; unchanged)
- Return on equity 15% or more: FAIL. About 6.8%, 6.8%, 7.7% and 6.3% for 2022/23–2025/26; about 6.3% for the last 12 months.
- Net debt no more than equity: PASS, just. 0.92x owners' equity at September 2026 (0.26x in March). About 5x EBITDA while the projects are being built, well above the usual 3x comfort level.
- Steady profit: PASS. Owners' profit Rs 1.48–1.79bn every year for five years, no losses.
- Profit into cash: PASS. Cash before working capital Rs 4.93bn against profit Rs 2.15bn in 2025/26, but no dividend for 2025/26.

MANAGEMENT AND PLANS
Management is turning a steady wind, solar and hydro owner into a battery-storage and large-solar developer, mostly on debt. So far it is delivering on time: Diya Janani floating solar and the first battery site were commissioned in September 2026, the other 12 battery sites are due by December 2026, Rividhanavi reached financial close for August 2027, and Safe Power wind is under construction for May 2027. Gearing (gross debt ÷ debt plus equity) is about 46%, near the top of the 25–50% target.

SHAREHOLDERS
Akbar Brothers (36.4%), the Hirdaramani group (23.0%) and Mona Exports (9.4%) control the company; related companies hold about 71% and the public 24.6%. Between March and September 2026, BBH-Tundra Shikari Global (39.0m shares, 2.9%) left the top 20 while BBH-Tundra Sustainable Frontier added 12.5m; the Managing Director added 0.5m. Shareholders rose from 6,836 to 9,195.

REQUIRED RETURN
Beta 0.78 (provisional): Damodaran's global renewable energy unlevered beta of 0.57, relevered for net debt at 0.48x market value. No local 5-year beta was found. Cost of equity = 8.24% + 0.78 × (4.2% + 6.08%) = 16.3% (bear 17.8%, bull 14.8%). Cost of debt 8.65% (interest paid Rs 1.01bn ÷ average debt Rs 11.67bn), 7.6% after tax. WACC 13.5% (bear 14.5%, bull 12.5%), with debt 32.6% of the total.

REINVESTMENT AND GROWTH
- 2025/26 capex booked Rs 1.72bn against depreciation Rs 2.00bn; reinvestment Rs 2.02bn including working capital and the Rs 0.46bn put into Rividhanavi. Reinvestment rate 83.9% × return on capital 8.2% = 6.8% supported growth. Assumed growth 0% / 3% / 6% for today's plants is within it.
- 2026/27 is a build year: Rs 12.7bn of capex and Rs 9.2bn of project advances in six months. This is growth capex (new battery, solar and wind capacity), judged on its return, and is valued at cost in the DCF, not by raising the growth rate.
- Maintenance capex: the company doesn't split it. Range Rs 2.4bn (bear; the calculator's Rs 3.2bn two-year average includes the Hiruras and Sooryashakthi builds) / Rs 2.0bn (depreciation) / Rs 1.88bn (depreciation less goodwill impairment and licence amortisation).
- R&D: not disclosed.
- Warnings: the projects are funded mainly by new borrowing (Rs 19bn in six months). Older turbines need repowering when contracts end.

VALUATION (Rs per share; bear / base / bull, weighted 30/50/20)
- Whole-company DCF plus projects and joint ventures: 2.86 / 9.88 / 18.91 (weighted 9.58). Today's plants: Rs 1.6 / 2.35 / 2.7bn a year of cash before interest after maintenance, after-tax operating profit Rs 2.10 / 2.48 / 2.71bn, growth 0/3/6% then 1/3/4%, WACC 14.5 / 13.5 / 12.5%: firm value Rs 10.5 / 15.8 / 22.0bn (48% / 62% / 74% from after year 5). Less net debt Rs 24.89bn; plus projects being built at 85% / 100% / 120% of their Rs 21.9bn cost and joint ventures at 85% / 100% / 125% of Rs 6.57bn book; less minorities Rs 5.94bn.
- P/E: 5.06 / 6.09 / 8.61 (weighted 6.29). EPS to March 2027 Rs 1.20 / 1.35 / 1.55 × justified P/E 4.24 / 4.51 / 5.53. The base EPS is far below the September quarter × 4 (Rs 2.52) because of the windy-season peak; it is 11% above the last 12 months' Rs 1.22.
- Justified P/B: 5.04 / 6.74 / 11.07 (weighted 7.10). ROE 6 / 7.5 / 10%, growth 2 / 3 / 4%.
- Residual income: 3.67 / 4.97 / 8.10 (weighted 5.21). ROE from 6.3% to 6 / 7.5 / 10%, below the cost of equity throughout; now from the shared calculator (on 17 November it was worked by hand and stopped after year 10, giving 10.84).
- Dividends: 1.58 / 3.87 / 9.83 (weighted 4.38). Rs 0.25 / 0.50 / 1.00 a year from now on, growing 2 / 4 / 6%. The dividend is at risk while cash goes into projects.
- Scenario averages: 3.64 / 6.31 / 11.30. Fair value Rs 6.51.

Ratio checks: beta 0.78, cost of equity 16.3% and WACC 13.5% are inside their normal ranges. Net debt/EBITDA of about 5x is above the usual 3x: the debt is for plants not yet earning, and should fall towards 3x if the battery and solar projects earn as planned. Maintenance capex is 1.0x depreciation in the base. Value after year 5 is under 75% in all cases. Long-run growth (1–4%) is below the 12.24% bond yield and WACC. ROE of 6–8% is below the 15% test; the justified P/E and P/B follow from it.

BUY PRICE
Fair value Rs 6.51. Buy at Rs 5.54 or less (15% margin), strong buy at Rs 4.88 or less (25%).
500-share plan: 200 at up to Rs 5.54, 150 at up to Rs 5.20, 150 at up to Rs 4.88; average about Rs 5.24, about Rs 2,620 in total (Rs 19,000 at Rs 38.00).
Realism: Rs 5.54 needs a fall of about 85%. The share traded at Rs 38.50–41.90 in the September quarter and Rs 22.90–56.10 in the year to March 2026. Not likely.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY VIEW
Higher: battery sites earning well above the cost of capital; Rividhanavi and Safe Power on time and budget, lifting ROE to 12% or more; older wind farms repowered or re-contracted on good terms; the CEB paying on time and paying curtailment compensation.
Lower: ROE staying at 6–8% after the new plants start; more debt or rising finance costs; wind contracts ending without replacement; more curtailment; cost overruns on Rividhanavi.

UNCERTAIN OR NOT FOUND
- Exact contract expiry dates for the older wind farms, battery storage tariffs and Rividhanavi's tariff aren't in the reports read.
- Beta is provisional (Damodaran's emerging-markets file blocked; no local 5-year betas found).
- Dividends before 2024/25 and opening equity for 2021/22 aren't in the reports read; EPS and ROE for 2021/22–2023/24 are worked out from the five-year summary.
